prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: flood defences and the premium. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 1)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When a home has a flood gate, airbrick covers or demountable barriers fitted and maintained, I should note that the premium can still reflect the broader flood exposure, but the practical claim response may be less severe if the defences are credible and in place before the event."},{"type":"fact","content":"When a member asks whether new flood defences will automatically reduce the premium, I should treat that as not guaranteed: pricing usually depends on the postcode, flood history and wider risk factors, not just one improvement."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the property sits in an area with repeated surface-water issues, I should remember that even good river defences do not remove the risk entirely, so the premium may stay elevated if local drainage remains a concern."},{"type":"preference","content":"When assessing a claim, I should prefer clear evidence of when the defences were installed or last serviced, because dated maintenance records help separate routine risk reduction from post-loss mitigation."},{"type":"fact","content":"When a member has invested in permanent flood resilience measures such as raised electrics or non-return valves, I should treat them as risk-reducing features, but not as a promise of a lower premium without underwriting review."},{"type":"observation","content":"When flood defences are temporary and need manual deployment, I should check whether the member can realistically use them in time, because a defence that is difficult to deploy adds less comfort to the risk assessment."},{"type":"fact","content":"When a property has no history of flooding but is protected by local authority or Environment Agency schemes, I should still reflect residual risk in the premium, since scheme performance and maintenance can vary over time."},{"type":"preference","content":"When I see a detailed flood report, I should favour objective sources such as flood maps, survey evidence and repair invoices over general reassurance, because precise evidence is better for both triage and pricing context."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a home is protected from fluvial flooding but vulnerable to blocked drains and heavy rain, I should remember that members often expect the premium to fall sharply, yet the claim pattern may still justify caution because escape-of-water and surface-water losses remain."},{"type":"fact","content":"When flood defences clearly reduce the expected severity of damage, I should record that they may support a more favourable underwriting view at renewal, but the premium change will usually be incremental rather than immediate or automatic."}]}
